narrative:
The model predicts you have a 45% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of success.

The decision rests mainly on three key factors. The most influential was your answer that you do not want to pursue higher education. Almost every student who passed expressed a clear desire to continue studying after school; your lack of that ambition strongly pulled the prediction toward failure. The second most important factor was your clean record of zero past class failures. This actually worked in your favor and pushed the prediction back toward passing. Finally, your very low weekend alcohol consumption also helped the model lean slightly toward a pass, since heavier drinkers in the data tended to struggle more.

Even though two of the top factors spoke in your favor, the absence of any stated goal for higher education outweighed them. Because the overall risk remains elevated, remedial courses are mandatory.

To improve, you should first reflect on why you no longer want to continue your studies and whether that view could change. Setting a clearer personal goal often motivates stronger effort. At the same time, keep protecting the positive habits you already have—maintaining zero failures and avoiding heavy drinking—while adding consistent weekly study time, which most successful students in your school manage at two to five hours. These small, steady changes can meaningfully raise your chances of passing.
